claim: Hsf1 and Hsp70 constitute a two-component feedback loop that regulates the yeast heat shock response
source: Hsf1 and Hsp70 constitute a two-component feedback loop that regulates the yeast heat shock response
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by experimental data including feedback loop severing experiments, binding assays, and mathematical modeling

claim: Hsp70 is the chaperone responsible for Hsf1 repression
source: Previously we identified Hsp70 as the chaperone responsible for Hsf1 repression and constructed a mathematical model that recapitulated the yeast heat shock response (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Dissociation of Hsp70 activates Hsf1
source: The model was based on two assumptions: dissociation of Hsp70 activates Hsf1, and transcriptional induction of Hsp70 deactivates Hsf1.
evidence: This is a model assumption that is validated through experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Transcriptional induction of Hsp70 deactivates Hsf1
source: The model was based on two assumptions: dissociation of Hsp70 activates Hsf1, and transcriptional induction of Hsp70 deactivates Hsf1.
evidence: This is a model assumption validated by feedback loop severing experiments

claim: Hsf1 was unable to efficiently deactivate in the absence of Hsp70 transcriptional induction
source: As predicted by the model, Hsf1 was unable to efficiently deactivate in the absence of Hsp70 transcriptional induction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the ∆FBL strain shown in Figure 1B

claim: CE2 is a discrete Hsp70 binding site on Hsf1
source: Next, we mapped a discrete Hsp70 binding site on Hsf1 to a C-terminal segment known as conserved element 2 (CE2).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation, in vitro binding assays, and fluorescence polarization data

claim: CE2 binds to Hsp70 with low affinity (9 µM) in vitro
source: In vitro, CE2 binds to Hsp70 with low affinity (9 µM), in agreement with model requirements.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Removal of CE2 resulted in increased basal Hsf1 activity
source: In cells, removal of CE2 resulted in increased basal Hsf1 activity and delayed deactivation during heat shock, while tandem repeats of CE2 sped up Hsf1 deactivation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring HSE-YFP reporter levels

claim: Removal of CE2 resulted in delayed deactivation during heat shock
source: In cells, removal of CE2 resulted in increased basal Hsf1 activity and delayed deactivation during heat shock, while tandem repeats of CE2 sped up Hsf1 deactivation.
evidence: Supported by heat shock time course data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Tandem repeats of CE2 sped up Hsf1 deactivation
source: In cells, removal of CE2 resulted in increased basal Hsf1 activity and delayed deactivation during heat shock, while tandem repeats of CE2 sped up Hsf1 deactivation.
evidence: Supported by heat shock time course data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The N-terminal domain of Hsf1 negatively regulates DNA binding
source: Finally, we uncovered a role for the N-terminal domain of Hsf1 in negatively regulating DNA binding.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing increased DNA binding in N-terminal deletion mutants

claim: The heat shock response is a transcriptional program conserved in eukaryotes from yeast to humans
source: The heat shock response is a transcriptional program conserved in eukaryotes from yeast to humans in which genes encoding molecular chaperones and other components of the protein homeostasis (proteostasis) machinery are activated to counteract proteotoxic stress (Anckar and Sistonen, 2011; Richter et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) is the master transcriptional regulator of the heat shock response
source: The master transcriptional regulator of the heat shock response, Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1), binds as a trimer to its cognate DNA motif – the heat shock element (HSE) – in the promoters and enhancers of its target genes (Gross et al., 1990; Hentze et al., 2016; Sorger and Nelson, 1989; Xiao et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Hsf1 binds as a trimer to the heat shock element (HSE)
source: The master transcriptional regulator of the heat shock response, Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1), binds as a trimer to its cognate DNA motif – the heat shock element (HSE) – in the promoters and enhancers of its target genes (Gross et al., 1990; Hentze et al., 2016; Sorger and Nelson, 1989; Xiao et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: In yeast, Hsf1 is essential under all conditions
source: In yeast, Hsf1 is essential under all conditions because it is required to drive the high level of basal chaperone expression needed to sustain growth (McDaniel et al., 1989; Solís et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Hsf1 is required to drive the high level of basal chaperone expression needed to sustain growth in yeast
source: In yeast, Hsf1 is essential under all conditions because it is required to drive the high level of basal chaperone expression needed to sustain growth (McDaniel et al., 1989; Solís et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Mammalian Hsf1 is dispensable under non-heat shock conditions
source: Mammalian Hsf1 is dispensable under non-heat shock conditions because it exclusively controls stress-inducible expression of its target regulon, while high-level basal chaperone expression is Hsf1-independent (Mahat et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: Mammalian Hsf1 exclusively controls stress-inducible expression of its target regulon
source: Mammalian Hsf1 is dispensable under non-heat shock conditions because it exclusively controls stress-inducible expression of its target regulon, while high-level basal chaperone expression is Hsf1-independent (Mahat et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: High-level basal chaperone expression is Hsf1-independent in mammals
source: Mammalian Hsf1 is dispensable under non-heat shock conditions because it exclusively controls stress-inducible expression of its target regulon, while high-level basal chaperone expression is Hsf1-independent (Mahat et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: Hsf1 plays pro-cancer roles both in tumor cells and the supporting stroma
source: Hsf1 has been shown to play pro-cancer roles both in tumor cells and the supporting stroma (Dai et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2007; Santagata et al., 2011; Scherz-Shouval et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Hsf1 takes on specialized transcriptional roles to support malignant growth
source: In addition to supplying high levels of chaperones to cancer cells, Hsf1 takes on specialized transcriptional roles to support malignant growth, and its activity is associated with poor prognosis in a range of human cancers (Mendillo et al., 2012; Santagata et al., 2011; Scherz-Shouval et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Hsf1 activity is associated with poor prognosis in a range of human cancers
source: In addition to supplying high levels of chaperones to cancer cells, Hsf1 takes on specialized transcriptional roles to support malignant growth, and its activity is associated with poor prognosis in a range of human cancers (Mendillo et al., 2012; Santagata et al., 2011; Scherz-Shouval et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Lack of Hsf1 activity has been proposed to contribute to the development of neurodegenerative diseases associated with protein aggregates
source: Conversely, lack of Hsf1 activity has been proposed to contribute to the development of neurodegenerative diseases associated with protein aggregates (Gomez-Pastor et al., 2017; Neef et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: A quantitative description of the regulatory mechanisms that control Hsf1 activity in any cell type remains lacking
source: Despite the potential therapeutic benefits of modulating Hsf1 activity, a quantitative description of the regulatory mechanisms that control its activity in any cell type remains lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work

claim: Binding and dissociation of the chaperone Hsp70 is the primary ON/OFF switch for Hsf1
source: Our recent work in Saccharomyces cerevisiae demonstrated that binding and dissociation of the chaperone Hsp70 is the primary ON/OFF switch for Hsf1, while phosphorylation is dispensable for activation but serves to amplify the transcriptional output (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Phosphorylation is dispensable for Hsf1 activation but serves to amplify the transcriptional output
source: Our recent work in Saccharomyces cerevisiae demonstrated that binding and dissociation of the chaperone Hsp70 is the primary ON/OFF switch for Hsf1, while phosphorylation is dispensable for activation but serves to amplify the transcriptional output (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: The mathematical model was able to recapitulate experimental data of Hsf1 activity during heat shock
source: While the model was able to recapitulate experimental data of Hsf1 activity during heat shock and correctly predicted the outcome of defined perturbations, its two central tenets remain untested
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and data in this manuscript

claim: The mathematical model correctly predicted the outcome of defined perturbations
source: While the model was able to recapitulate experimental data of Hsf1 activity during heat shock and correctly predicted the outcome of defined perturbations, its two central tenets remain untested
evidence: Supported by experimental validation of model predictions shown in Figure 1B

claim: When the temperature is raised, the concentration of unfolded proteins exceeds the capacity of Hsp70
source: When the temperature is raised, the concentration of unfolded proteins exceeds the capacity of Hsp70.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on established understanding of heat shock response

claim: Hsp70 is titrated away from Hsf1 during heat shock
source: Hsp70 is titrated away from Hsf1, freeing Hsf1 to induce more Hsp70.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by previous work cited in the manuscript

claim: Once sufficient Hsp70 has been produced to restore proteostasis, Hsp70 binds and deactivates Hsf1
source: Once sufficient Hsp70 has been produced to restore proteostasis, Hsp70 binds and deactivates Hsf1.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by experimental data in this manuscript

claim: The ∆FBL strain activated the reporter with identical kinetics to the wild type during the early phase of the response
source: As predicted by the simulation, the ∆FBL strain activated the reporter with identical kinetics to the wild type during the early phase of the response, but failed to attenuate induction during prolonged exposure to elevated temperature (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The ∆FBL strain failed to attenuate induction during prolonged exposure to elevated temperature
source: As predicted by the simulation, the ∆FBL strain activated the reporter with identical kinetics to the wild type during the early phase of the response, but failed to attenuate induction during prolonged exposure to elevated temperature (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The model underestimated the amount of time required to observe the separation between the wild type and ∆FBL strains
source: While the simulation correctly predicted the experimental results qualitatively, the model underestimated the amount of time required to observe the separation between the wild type and ∆FBL strains, suggesting the strength of the feedback had been exaggerated in the first iteration of the model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data

claim: The strength of the feedback had been exaggerated in the first iteration of the model
source: While the simulation correctly predicted the experimental results qualitatively, the model underestimated the amount of time required to observe the separation between the wild type and ∆FBL strains, suggesting the strength of the feedback had been exaggerated in the first iteration of the model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between model and experimental data

claim: By reducing the strength of the feedback loop, the model was able to quantitatively match the behavior of both the wild type and ∆FBL cells
source: By reducing the strength of the feedback loop, we were able to quantitatively match the behavior of both the wild type and ∆FBL cells (Figure 1B, see Materials and methods for the updated parameter value).
evidence: Supported by updated model simulations shown in Figure 1B

claim: The wild type and ∆FBL strains grew equally at 30°C
source: By contrast, the wild type and ∆FBL strains grew equally at 30°C, and the ∆FBL strain showed only a slight reduction in growth at 37°C (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The ∆FBL strain showed only a slight reduction in growth at 37°C
source: By contrast, the wild type and ∆FBL strains grew equally at 30°C, and the ∆FBL strain showed only a slight reduction in growth at 37°C (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The ssa1/2∆ cells displayed severely impaired growth at 30°C and were inviable at 37°C
source: The ssa1/2∆ cells – which retain viability due to Hsf1-mediated induction of SSA3/4 – displayed severely impaired growth at 30°C and were inviable at 37°C (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Removal of both SSA3 and SSA4 had only modest phenotypic consequences at elevated temperature
source: Surprisingly, removal of both SSA3 and SSA4 – the major heat shock-inducible Hsp70 genes in yeast – had only modest phenotypic consequences at elevated temperature.
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Upon acute heat shock, the number of Hsp104-mKate foci spiked in both wild type and ∆FBL cells
source: Upon acute heat shock, the number of Hsp104-mKate foci spiked in both wild type and ∆FBL cells, but dissolved with the same kinetics in both strains (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: Hsp104-mKate foci dissolved with the same kinetics in both wild type and ∆FBL strains
source: Upon acute heat shock, the number of Hsp104-mKate foci spiked in both wild type and ∆FBL cells, but dissolved with the same kinetics in both strains (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: The ∆FBL cells can restore proteostasis just as efficiently as wild type cells
source: These data suggest that the ∆FBL cells can restore proteostasis just as efficiently as wild type cells and that the prolonged Hsf1 activation in the ∆FBL cells is due to a spdeactivation defect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hsp104-mKate foci dissolution data

claim: The prolonged Hsf1 activation in the ∆FBL cells is due to a deactivation defect
source: These data suggest that the ∆FBL cells can restore proteostasis just as efficiently as wild type cells and that the prolonged Hsf1 activation in the ∆FBL cells is due to a spdeactivation defect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of proteostasis restoration and sustained Hsf1 activity

claim: Hsp104 requires Hsp70 for efficient activity
source: Since Hsp104 requires Hsp70 for efficient activity (Seyffer et al., 2012; Winkler et al., 2012), there must be sufficient Hsp70 expressed under basal conditions to allow Hsp104 to operate.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: There must be sufficient Hsp70 expressed under basal conditions to allow Hsp104 to operate in ∆FBL cells
source: Since Hsp104 requires Hsp70 for efficient activity (Seyffer et al., 2012; Winkler et al., 2012), there must be sufficient Hsp70 expressed under basal conditions to allow Hsp104 to operate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Hsp104 functions normally in ∆FBL cells

claim: The transcriptional negative feedback loop is required to deactivate Hsf1 once proteostasis has been restored
source: While Hsp104 may not recognize all classes of unfolded proteins and aggregates, these results suggest that the transcriptional negative feedback loop is required to deactivate Hsf1 once proteostasis has been restored.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ∆FBL experimental results

claim: Removal of the N-terminal region led to significantly increased Hsf1 activity under both non-heat shock and heat shock conditions
source: As previously shown, removal of the N-terminal region led to significantly increased Hsf1 activity under both non-heat shock and heat shock conditions in this assay (Sorger, 1990; Zheng et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 2A

claim: Removal of the C-terminal region significantly reduced Hsf1 activity under both non-heat shock and heat shock conditions
source: while removal of the C-terminal region significantly reduced Hsf1 activity under both conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In the N-terminal region, two distinct 12 amino acid segments when deleted resulted in increased Hsf1 activity (amino acids 85–96 and 121–132)
source: In the N-terminal region, we found two distinct 12 amino acid segments that when deleted resulted in increased Hsf1 activity (amino acids 85–96 and 121–132) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by scanning mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In the C-terminal region, removal of two consecutive 12 amino acid segments as well as truncation of the final six amino acids resulted in increased Hsf1 activity (amino acids 528–539, 540–551 and 828–833)
source: In the C-terminal region, removal of two consecutive 12 amino acid segments as well as truncation of the final six amino acids resulted in increased Hsf1 activity (amino acids 528–539, 540–551 and 828–833) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by scanning mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Combining the N-terminal deletions (∆85–96/∆121–132) resulted in a mutant with significantly greater basal activity than either of the single mutants
source: Combining the N-terminal deletions (∆85–96/∆121–132) resulted in a mutant with significantly greater basal activity than either of the single mutants, suggesting that these segments operate independently to repress Hsf1 activity (p<0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The N-terminal segments N1 and N2 operate independently to repress Hsf1 activity
source: Combining the N-terminal deletions (∆85–96/∆121–132) resulted in a mutant with significantly greater basal activity than either of the single mutants, suggesting that these segments operate independently to repress Hsf1 activity (p<0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the additive effect of the double deletion

claim: Combining the consecutive C-terminal segments (∆528–539/∆540–551) resulted in a double mutant with the same activity as the single deletions
source: By contrast, combining the consecutive C-terminal segments (∆528–539/∆540–551) resulted in a double mutant with the same activity as the single deletions, suggesting that a unique functional determinant encompasses these segments (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: A unique functional determinant encompasses the C-terminal segments 528-551
source: By contrast, combining the consecutive C-terminal segments (∆528–539/∆540–551) resulted in a double mutant with the same activity as the single deletions, suggesting that a unique functional determinant encompasses these segments (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-additive effect of the double deletion

claim: A region spanning segments 528-551 comprises a previously identified element conserved in Hsf1 in other fungal species known as 'conserved element 2' (CE2)
source: Consistent with this notion, a region spanning these two segments comprises a previously identified element conserved in Hsf1 in other fungal species known as 'conserved element 2' (CE2) (Figure 2B) (Jakobsen and Pelham, 1991; Nicholls et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B

claim: Specific removal of CE2 was sufficient to match the increased level of Hsf1 activity observed in the ∆528–539/∆540–551 mutant
source: Indeed, specific removal of CE2 was sufficient to match the increased level of Hsf1 activity observed in the ∆528–539/∆540–551 mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Combining the N1/N2 and CE2 deletions resulted in an Hsf1 mutant with significantly greater activity than either the ∆N1/∆N2 mutant or the ∆CE2 mutant
source: However, combining the N1/N2 and CE2 deletions resulted in an Hsf1 mutant with significantly greater activity than either the ∆N1/∆N2 mutant or the ∆CE2 mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The scanning mutagenesis revealed three independent repressive segments on Hsf1 (N1, N2, and CE2)
source: Together, the scanning mutagenesis revealed three independent repressive segments on Hsf1 (N1, N2, and CE2).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the mutagenesis data

claim: Under non-heat shock conditions, wild type Hsf1 binding ranged over nearly two orders of magnitude across target promoters
source: Under non-heat shock conditions, wild type Hsf1 binding ranged over nearly two orders of magnitude across these targets, from 0.14% of input at the TMA10 promoter to 12.0% of input at the 4xHSE promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Upon acute heat shock, the inducibility of Hsf1 binding varied widely across target promoters
source: Upon acute heat shock, the inducibility of Hsf1 binding also varied widely across these targets, with induction of greater than 100-fold for TMA10 and less than 1.5-fold for HSC82 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Hsf1 is not constitutively bound to its target genes
source: These data are inconsistent with the notion that Hsf1 is constitutively bound to its target genes (Gross et al., 1990; Jakobsen and Pelham, 1988; Sorger et al., 1987).
evidence: This is an inference based on the variable binding observed in ChIP experiments

claim: The Hsf1∆N mutant showed significantly increased association with the 4xHSE and SSA4 promoters under non-heat shock conditions
source: Interestingly, the Hsf1∆N mutant showed significantly increased association with the 4xHSE and SSA4 promoters under non-heat shock conditions (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Increased binding to the 4xHSE promoter was accompanied by increased transcriptional output of the YFP reporter in Hsf1∆N cells
source: This increased binding to the 4xHSE promoter was accompanied by increased transcriptional output of the YFP reporter in Hsf1∆N cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The N-terminal region of Hsf1 inhibits DNA binding and thereby reduces transcriptional activity
source: These data suggest a simple relationship between DNA binding and transcription for the Hsf1∆N mutant: the N-terminal region of Hsf1 inhibits DNA binding and thereby reduces transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between increased DNA binding and increased transcription in the ∆N mutant

claim: The Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 mutant mirrored Hsf1∆N in both its increased binding to the 4xHSE promoter and increased transcription of the YFP reporter under non-heat shock conditions relative to wild type
source: Consistent with a role for the N-terminal segment in regulating DNA binding, the Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 mutant mirrored Hsf1∆N in both its increased binding to the 4xHSE promoter and increased transcription of the YFP reporter under non-heat shock conditions relative to wild type (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 showed no increase in association with the SSA4 promoter compared to wild type
source: However, unlike the complete ablation of the N-terminal region, Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 showed no increase in association with the SSA4 promoter compared to wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that its enhanced association with endogenous targets may be limited.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The enhanced association of Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 with endogenous targets may be limited
source: However, unlike the complete ablation of the N-terminal region, Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 showed no increase in association with the SSA4 promoter compared to wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that its enhanced association with endogenous targets may be limited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects at different promoters

claim: Neither Hsf1∆CE2 nor Hsf1∆N1/∆N2/∆CE2 showed significant differences compared to wild type at any of the six target promoters under either non-heat shock or heat shock conditions
source: Neither Hsf1∆CE2 nor Hsf1∆N1/∆N2/∆CE2 showed significant differences compared to wild type at any of the six target promoters under either non-heat shock or heat shock conditions, indicating that CE2 has no effect on Hsf1 DNA binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: CE2 has no effect on Hsf1 DNA binding
source: Neither Hsf1∆CE2 nor Hsf1∆N1/∆N2/∆CE2 showed significant differences compared to wild type at any of the six target promoters under either non-heat shock or heat shock conditions, indicating that CE2 has no effect on Hsf1 DNA binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of difference in ChIP signal

claim: Under heat shock conditions, none of the five mutants showed significant differences in binding to the 4xHSE promoter compared to wild type
source: Remarkably, under heat shock conditions, none of the five mutants showed significant differences in binding to the 4xHSE promoter compared to wild type (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A

claim: During heat shock, the differences in YFP reporter levels reflect the different transactivation abilities of the series of mutants
source: Thus, during heat shock, the differences in YFP reporter levels reflect the different transactivation abilities of the series of mutants, spanning more than 16-fold between Hsf1∆C and Hsf1∆N1/∆N2/∆CE2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that DNA binding is similar but transcription differs

claim: The N-terminal region inhibits DNA binding at select promoters with a major contribution from the N1 and N2 segments
source: Taken together, the ChIP results suggest that the N-terminal region inhibits DNA binding at select promoters with a major contribution from the N1 and N2 segments.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the ChIP data

claim: The effect of the N-terminal region on DNA binding may be direct, reflecting an intrinsically higher affinity of Hsf1∆N or Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 for DNA
source: This effect may be direct, reflecting an intrinsically higher affinity of Hsf1∆N or Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 for DNA, or indirect, a consequence of enhanced ability to recruit chromatin remodeling enzymes to open local chromatin structure.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: The effect of the N-terminal region on DNA binding may be indirect, a consequence of enhanced ability to recruit chromatin remodeling enzymes to open local chromatin structure
source: This effect may be direct, reflecting an intrinsically higher affinity of Hsf1∆N or Hsf1∆N1/∆N2 for DNA, or indirect, a consequence of enhanced ability to recruit chromatin remodeling enzymes to open local chromatin structure.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: Removal of the entire N-terminal region or the N1/N2 segments had no effect on Hsp70 binding relative to wild type
source: Removal of the entire N-terminal region or the N1/N2 segments had no effect on Hsp70 binding relative to wild type (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by IP/MS data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Removal of the full C-terminal region significantly reduced the association of Hsf1 with Hsp70
source: By contrast, removal of the full C-terminal region significantly reduced the association of Hsf1 with Hsp70 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by IP/MS data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Specific removal of CE2 resulted in significantly diminished association with Hsp70
source: Moreover, specific removal of CE2 – either alone or in combination with the N1/N2 deletions – also resulted in significantly diminished association with Hsp70, nearly matching removal of the entire C-terminal region (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by IP/MS data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The residual Hsp70 that co-precipitated with Hsf1∆CE2 was refractory to dissociation upon heat shock
source: The residual Hsp70 that co-precipitated with Hsf1∆CE2 was refractory to dissociation upon heat shock, suggesting that this secondary interaction is unlikely to be regulatory (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The secondary Hsp70 interaction with Hsf1∆CE2 is unlikely to be regulatory
source: The residual Hsp70 that co-precipitated with Hsf1∆CE2 was refractory to dissociation upon heat shock, suggesting that this secondary interaction is unlikely to be regulatory (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of heat shock-dependent dissociation

claim: The Hsf1R537E,K541D,R543E triple mutant (ce2-mut) displayed increased levels of the HSE-YFP reporter under non-heat shock conditions, phenocopying ∆CE2
source: Indeed, the Hsf1R537E,K541D,R543E triple mutant (referred to as ce2-mut) displayed increased levels of the HSE-YFP reporter under non-heat shock conditions, phenocopying ∆CE2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Introduction of two additional repeats of the wild type CE2 sequence (3xCE2) into Hsf1 reduced the basal level of the reporter
source: Conversely, introduction of two additional repeats of the wild type CE2 sequence (3xCE2) into Hsf1 reduced the basal level of the reporter (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Wild type Hsf1-6xHIS was able to outcompete wild type Hsf1-V5 for binding to Ssa2 at 5-fold molar excess
source: Whereas wild type Hsf1-6xHIS was able to outcompete wild type Hsf1-V5 for binding to Ssa2 (the most highly expressed yeast Hsp70) at 5-fold molar excess, Hsf1∆CE2-6xHIS was not (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Hsf1∆CE2-6xHIS was not able to outcompete wild type Hsf1-V5 for binding to Ssa2 at 5-fold molar excess
source: Whereas wild type Hsf1-6xHIS was able to outcompete wild type Hsf1-V5 for binding to Ssa2 (the most highly expressed yeast Hsp70) at 5-fold molar excess, Hsf1∆CE2-6xHIS was not (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4D

claim: CE2 is necessary for Hsp70 to bind to Hsf1 and repress its basal activity
source: Together, these results demonstrate that CE2 is necessary for Hsp70 to bind to Hsf1 and repress its basal activity.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: Ssa2 directly binds to CE2 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 9 µM
source: Using this assay, we determined that Ssa2 directly binds to CE2 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 9 µM, while the Kd for the ce2-mut peptide is reduced more than 5-fold (extrapolated to be 52 µM).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The Kd for the ce2-mut peptide binding to Ssa2 is reduced more than 5-fold (extrapolated to be 52 µM)
source: Using this assay, we determined that Ssa2 directly binds to CE2 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 9 µM, while the Kd for the ce2-mut peptide is reduced more than 5-fold (extrapolated to be 52 µM).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Addition of a single CE2 sequence to mKate modestly but significantly increased the HSE-YFP level
source: Addition of a single CE2 sequence to mKate modestly but significantly increased the HSE-YFP level, while addition of two or three tandem CE2 segments dramatically induced the HSE-YFP reporter, to a greater extent than even the NHsf1-CHsf1 decoy (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by decoy assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Addition of two or three tandem CE2 segments dramatically induced the HSE-YFP reporter, to a greater extent than even the NHsf1-CHsf1 decoy
source: Addition of a single CE2 sequence to mKate modestly but significantly increased the HSE-YFP level, while addition of two or three tandem CE2 segments dramatically induced the HSE-YFP reporter, to a greater extent than even the NHsf1-CHsf1 decoy (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by decoy assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: No induction was observed for the ce2-mut decoys, even in the presence of three tandem repeats
source: By contrast, no induction was observed for the ce2-mut decoys, even in the presence of three tandem repeats (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by decoy assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Both in vitro and in cells, CE2 is sufficient to bind to Hsp70
source: Thus, both in vitro and in cells, CE2 is sufficient to bind to Hsp70.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on fluorescence polarization and decoy assay data

claim: Simulations in which affinity was increased showed faster deactivation kinetics and a lower maximal output
source: Intuitively, simulations in which we increased the affinity showed faster deactivation kinetics and a lower maximal output, while decreasing the affinity showed slower deactivation and increased maximal output (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Simulations in which affinity was decreased showed slower deactivation and increased maximal output
source: Intuitively, simulations in which we increased the affinity showed faster deactivation kinetics and a lower maximal output, while decreasing the affinity showed slower deactivation and increased maximal output (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Hsf13xCE2 deactivated more rapidly than wild type
source: In agreement with the model, Hsf13xCE2 deactivated more rapidly than wild type, while Hsf1∆CE2 and Hsf1ce2-mut displayed delayed deactivation kinetics in a heat shock time course (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental heat shock time course data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Hsf1∆CE2 and Hsf1ce2-mut displayed delayed deactivation kinetics in a heat shock time course
source: In agreement with the model, Hsf13xCE2 deactivated more rapidly than wild type, while Hsf1∆CE2 and Hsf1ce2-mut displayed delayed deactivation kinetics in a heat shock time course (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental heat shock time course data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: The affinity for Hsp70 tunes Hsf1 activation dynamics
source: Thus, the affinity for Hsp70 tunes Hsf1 activation dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the correlation between affinity changes and dynamics

claim: The model was remarkably powerful in its ability to predict the dynamics of Hsf1 activity when challenged with targeted perturbations to the system architecture
source: Moreover, we found the model to be remarkably powerful in its ability to predict the dynamics of Hsf1 activity when challenged with targeted perturbations to the system architecture despite its oversimplified structure.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the agreement between model predictions and experimental results

claim: Conceptualizing the heat shock response as a two-component feedback loop is an appropriate abstraction that captures the essence of the regulatory network
source: These results argue that conceptualizing the heat shock response as a two-component feedback loop – in which Hsf1 positively regulates Hsp70 expression and Hsp70 negatively regulates Hsf1 activity – is an appropriate abstraction that captures the essence of the regulatory network.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the success of the simplified model

claim: Whether this simplifying abstraction can be applied to HSF1 regulation in metazoans remains to be determined
source: Whether this simplifying abstraction can be applied to HSF1 regulation in metazoans remains to be determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current work

claim: The amino acid composition of CE2, consisting of hydrophobic and basic residues, is reminiscent of peptide sequences known to bind to Hsp70 in vitro
source: Its amino acid composition, consisting of hydrophobic and basic residues, is reminiscent of peptide sequences known to bind to Hsp70 in vitro (Van Durme et al., 2009), though the affinity we measured (9 µM) is relatively weak.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature and comparison to measured affinity

claim: The weak affinity of CE2 for Hsp70 is likely necessary to allow for stress-dependent dissociation of the complex
source: Given the stoichiometry of Hsp70:Hsf1 in cells (>500:1) (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2003) this weak affinity is likely necessary to allow for stress-dependent dissociation of the complex and has been a constant requirement of our mathematical model since its inception (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the stoichiometry and model requirements

claim: The stoichiometry of Hsp70:Hsf1 in cells is greater than 500:1
source: Given the stoichiometry of Hsp70:Hsf1 in cells (>500:1) (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2003) this weak affinity is likely necessary to allow for stress-dependent dissociation of the complex and has been a constant requirement of our mathematical model since its inception (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: While CE2 is not conserved in mammalian genomes in primary sequence, it would seem facile to evolve a distinct but functionally analogous hydrophobic and basic segment to allow for weak Hsp70 binding
source: Thus, while CE2 is not conserved in mammalian genomes in primary sequence, it would seem facile to evolve a distinct but functionally analogous hydrophobic and basic segment to allow for weak Hsp70 binding.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms

claim: The N-terminus of Hsf1 has a transactivation function and is important for efficient recruitment of Mediator during heat shock
source: While removal of the N-terminal region of Hsf1 leads to increased activity, at least in certain genomic contexts (Sorger, 1990) – suggesting that this region is repressive – the N-terminus also has a transactivation function and is important for efficient recruitment of Mediator during heat shock (Kim and Gross, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: Removal of the full N-terminal region results in increased association with select target gene promoters under non-heat shock conditions
source: Here we show that removal of the full N-terminal region results in increased association with select target gene promoters under non-heat shock conditions (Figure 3A), indicating a context-dependent role for this yeast-specific region in regulating DNA binding and suggesting a mechanistic basis for the increased transcriptional activity of Hsf1∆N relative to wild type Hsf1.
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The N-terminal region has a context-dependent role in regulating DNA binding
source: Here we show that removal of the full N-terminal region results in increased association with select target gene promoters under non-heat shock conditions (Figure 3A), indicating a context-dependent role for this yeast-specific region in regulating DNA binding and suggesting a mechanistic basis for the increased transcriptional activity of Hsf1∆N relative to wild type Hsf1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective increase in DNA binding at certain promoters

claim: Hsf1 can exist in one of four states in the yeast nucleus
source: Putting our observations together, we propose that Hsf1 can exist in one of four states in the yeast nucleus (Figure 7):
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings

claim: The dual mechanisms of Hsf1 regulation – control of DNA binding and accessibility of the transactivation domain – combine to exert exquisite quantitative control over Hsf1 activity
source: The dual mechanisms of Hsf1 regulation described here – control of DNA binding and accessibility of the transactivation domain – in addition to the fine-tuning capacity we previously demonstrated for phosphorylation (Zheng et al., 2016), combine to exert exquisite quantitative control over the Hsf1 activity and the expression of its target gene regulon.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings of this work and previous work

claim: These regulatory mechanisms enable cells to precisely tailor an optimal response to a variety of environmental and internal stresses
source: We propose that these regulatory mechanisms enable cells to precisely tailor an optimal response to a variety of environmental and internal stresses.
evidence: This is a proposed functional consequence of the regulatory mechanisms

claim: Wild type cells were able to increase Hsp70 levels during heat shock
source: As expected, wild type cells were able to increase Hsp70 levels during heat shock.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C

claim: ∆FBL cells were unable to induce Hsp70 during heat shock
source: By contrast, ∆FBL cells were unable to induce Hsp70 during heat shock, though the Hsp70 level was constitutively elevated (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The Hsp70 level was constitutively elevated in ∆FBL cells
source: By contrast, ∆FBL cells were unable to induce Hsp70 during heat shock, though the Hsp70 level was constitutively elevated (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Hsp104 is a disaggregase that forms puncta marking protein aggregates when tagged with a fluorescent protein
source: Hsp104 is a disaggregase that forms puncta marking protein aggregates when tagged with a fluorescent protein (Solís et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: SSA3 and SSA4 are the major heat shock-inducible Hsp70 genes in yeast
source: Surprisingly, removal of both SSA3 and SSA4 – the major heat shock-inducible Hsp70 genes in yeast – had only modest phenotypic consequences at elevated temperature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast Hsp70 genes

claim: Ssa2 is the most highly expressed yeast Hsp70
source: Whereas wild type Hsf1-6xHIS was able to outcompete wild type Hsf1-V5 for binding to Ssa2 (the most highly expressed yeast Hsp70) at 5-fold molar excess, Hsf1∆CE2-6xHIS was not (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast Hsp70 expression
